newsitem.title: USA: Key Whitewater figure McDougal sentencing Monday.
newsitem.headline: Key Whitewater figure McDougal sentencing Monday.

text.p: James McDougal, a former business partner of President Bill Clinton and the central figure in the Whitewater investigation, is to be sentenced on Monday on 18 counts of fraud and conspiracy.

McDougal, 56, faces up to 84 years in prison and fines of up to $4.5 million but prosecutors could recommend a reduced sentence if they believe he has sufficiently cooperated with their investigation into the finances of Clinton and a long list of Arkansas business and political figures.
"I'm a fatalist. I'm always prepared for the worst," McDougal told Reuters on Friday. "Whatever happens couldn't be much worse that what's already happened."

Sam Heuer, McDougal's attorney, said the prosecuting team of Whitewater investigator Kenneth Starr has agreed to advise Judge George Howard Jr. of the extent of McDougal's cooperation in recent months.
"I guess we'll see," said Heuer, when asked if he thought the prosecutors would recommend a reduced sentence.
Throughout his trial, McDougal vowed never to cooperate with the prosecutors, who he described as "Republican henchmen" on a mission to "destroy" Clinton's administration.
But within weeks of his conviction last May, McDougal began meeting with the prosecutors and his sentencing has since been postponed three times at Starr's request.
McDougal testified before a federal grand jury at least twice in the last two weeks. Prosecutors could request another postponement on Monday morning but that is considered unlikely.

McDougal has been the central figure in the Whitewater investigation from the very start. The owner of a Little Rock-based Madison Guaranty Savings and Loan, he persuaded the Clintons in 1978 to join him as partners in an ill-fated residential development in north Arkansas called Whitewater.

Madison Guaranty was declared insolvent and seized by federal regulators in 1989. Starr's team is trying to determine if Madison funds were illegally diverted to keep afloat the Whitewater project, which also ultimately failed.

In McDougal's trial last year, a prosecution witness testified that Clinton pressured him to make an illegal $300,000 loan to McDougal's wife, and prosecutors said about $50,000 of the proceeds were diverted to Whitewater.
In videotaped testimony, Clinton flatly denied any knowledge of the loan. McDougal also testified Clinton did nothing wrong but he reportedly changed his story after his conviction.
McDougal was also a key player in several other real estate ventures that captured Starr's interest, including a mobile home park near Little Rock called Castle Grande.
First Lady Hillary Clinton has acknowledged performing some legal work for the Castle Grande project, which federal regulators called a "sham transaction", but she denies any wrongdoing.
Convicted along with McDougal last May were his former wife Susan McDougal and Arkansas Gov. Jim Guy Tucker, who succeeded Clinton in the Arkansas statehouse.
Tucker was fined heavily and was forced to resign when convicted but escaped a prison sentence because of his deteriorating health.

Susan McDougal was sentenced to two years in prison and is serving a contempt of court sentence because she refused to answer questions before a Whitewater grand jury. She alleged prosecutors were forcing James McDougal to invent testimony against Clinton.

McDougal declined to discuss the information he has given Starr's team, and said he did not know what recommendations the prosecuting team would make on Monday. "This is a time for prayer and meditation," he said.
